Ladybird ditching a bunch of self developed libraries for production grade ones (like sqlite or skia) helped them immensely improve their browser.

Their goal for a while has been to make a production capable browser which is not owned or funded by Google. At the moment your choices are either Chromium based (owned by Google), Gecko or Safari based (both of which have deals with Google).

This is a fully independent engine funded by no-strings-attached sponsorships.

It's a good model, considering they've demonstrated that a full browser can be developed on a shoe-string compared to the competition.
To have a serious working browser alternative?
Is it serious? It doesn't seem particularly so.
I'm not sure about sqlite.... the way chrome handles it, well, it sucks and slow.

Sounds like poorly optimized in Chrome level. Should not be problem at all for sqlite
SQLite can handle many gigabytes worth of data so probsbly just a missing index or similar.

It might limit performance under linux maybe?

I can't get chromium browsers to have as good rendering as firefox no matter I try. My main use case is PDFs and whatsapp web so maybe it works differently with other things.

Not only that but also fully embracing LLM driven development has greatly enhanced the pace of progress in Ladybird, while other open source projects are in full denial mode coping with some silly excuses that AI isn't the future of programming, Ladybird team just chose to get shit done instead.

Copyright provenance is a real concern though, and that's the reason for a lot of the reluctance, for example in the GNU project. Oh, and there not being any LLM models that yet fulfill the criteria for free software.

Spam contributions have also been cited, but those should be easy enough to handle, at least once the aforementioned free models become available.

[delayed]

It's awesome to see an alternative browser being made that's not linked with Google's ads. With the security concerns that they're upfront about on this.

What precautions should I be taking as a user when using this while it's still in Alpha. My assumption would be just to use for any general web browsing that doesn't require login/auth/payments/downloads?

Running an insecure browser makes the whole OS on which the browser runs insecure. Don't assume anything on that OS will be kept private from attackers. Don't assume any other program on the OS hasn't been compromised.

BTW the chances of Ladybird ever becoming secure enough that you won't need the aforemention precautions is essentially zero unless a megacorporation adopts it like Apple once adopted KHTML (and turned it into WebKit/Safari).
This is a bit much, no? Your browser is not running as root and it's not executing arbitrary binaries.
But your browser is running as your own user, which can read everything you can, and if an RCE is found in Ladybird, it IS an arbitrary binary.

CVE-2026-106426 Race condition in Fonts in Google Chrome prior to 155.0.8059.39 allowed a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page.

CVE-2026-95311 Free of non-heap memory in Fonts in Google Chrome prior to 154.0.8037.57 allowed a remote attacker leveraging social engineering to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page.

These are in Chrome which has vastly more resources both red and blue teaming it. Though, Ladybird may have a security through obscurity advantage.

It doesn't appear that either has a POC, but RCE to root is just one more step, and really if you've got RCE you don't necessarily need root for exfil, DDOS participation, residential proxying, distributed scraping...

But not necessarily, one such precaution could be running the browser as a separate user and relying on FS permissions and the kernel for 'sandboxing'. Not impenetrable by any means (especially with all the recent Linux privesc disclosures of late), but still a solid (and simple) approach.

Related:

https://wiki.gentoo.org/wiki/Simple_sandbox

Are you aware that OpenAI recently found 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux?

https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/

It runs arbitrary JavaScript, which can oftentimes lead to remote code execution.

Moreover, in our mostly single-user 2026 operating systems, "not running as root" does not protect you from malware leaking personal files, saved credentials, SSH keys, cookies, passwords, etc.
I already bubblewrap my Firefox and you should do the same. Browsers are simply way too complex for their own good.
You sound like you would get an aneurysm if I told you my phone's bootloader is unlocked.
Nice to see the next goalpost move

So yeah, better avoid sending credentials with it, for now.

It's not the credentials that's the problem. It's visiting untrusted website that could compromise your browser and / or your whole OS.

And untrusted websites is basically the whole web.

If you're only visiting trusted sites (and that probably means only sites written by yourself), sending credentials should not be the problem here.
